entries.modern_form: PIE *mer- 'to rub away, wear down, harm' and *mer- 'to die' (Pokorny 4. mer- 'sterben' and 5. mer- 'reiben, wischen', pp. 735-737), with the extensions *mer-d-, *mer-k-, *mer-s-, the o-grade *mor-to- 'mortal, man' and the s-mobile variant *(s)merd- (Pokorny smerd- p. 970)
entries.note: Root, language label and glosses are right. Pokorny prints two lemmas, 4. mer- 'to die' (p. 735) and 5. mer- 'to rub, wipe; to pack, rob' (pp. 735-737), but closes the second with 'See also: identical with mer-4'; Watkins (AHD mer-2) merges them the same way ('Possibly the same root, but more likely distinct, is *mer-, to die'), so Nourai's single box 'Mer 2 ... to rub away, harm, die' follows the standard handbooks. The sub-labels are Pokorny's own extensions: mer-d- (Skt. mardati, Lat. mordeo), mer-k- (Skt. marcayati, Av. mahrka- 'death'), mor-to- ('mor-to- perishable: Skt. marta-, Av. maSa-, OP martiya-'). The one inaccuracy is the reference for 'Smerd: painful': Pokorny's p. 970 lemma is smerd- 'to stink'; the 'pain' words (OHG smerzan, smerzo, Gk. smerdnos, Eng. smart) stand on pp. 736-737 under mer-d-, and p. 970 only cross-refers to them ('smerd- to stink is a probably already Indo-European specialised use from (s)merd- in NHG schmerzen, Lat. mordere, see mer-, merd- above p. 736 f').

nodes.derivation: Of the four Latin words only mors is certain: mors, gen. mortis 'death' is the zero-grade *mr-ti- of *mer- 'to die' (= Skt. mrti-, Av. mereti-, Lith. mirtis, OCS su-mrti; Pokorny 735, Klein s.v. mortal). mortarium 'pounding bowl; the stuff pounded in it' is taken by Watkins as a suffixed zero-grade *mr-to- 'ground down' and de Vaan calls that plausible (from Proto-Italic *morto- < *mrto-), but Ernout-Meillet say flatly 'Aucune etymologie sure'. mordere 'to bite' is put by Pokorny and Klein under an extension *merd- (= Skt. mardati, mrdnati 'grinds, crushes', Gk. smerdnos 'terrible'), whereas Ernout-Meillet warn 'Aucun rapprochement sur ... On ne cite aucune racine indo-europeenne signifiant nettement mordre' and Watkins hedges with 'Possibly extended root *merd-'. morbus 'disease' was analysed as *mor-bho- 'that which consumes' (Pokorny 736, Klein), but Watkins adds 'but more likely of unknown origin' and Ernout-Meillet judge 'La ressemblance avec morior doit etre fortuite ... ce qui rend vain de chercher l'etymologie de morbus' (de Vaan: perhaps to mori 'look like death', or a non-IE word). Nourai's hyphenated spelling môr-târium is his own morpheme division of the Latin lemma mortarium.
nodes.derivation_fa: از این چهار واژهٔ لاتینی تنها mors «مرگ» (ستاک mort-) بی‌گمان از صورت ضعیف *mr̥-ti- ریشهٔ *mer- «مردن» است و با mṛti- سنسکریت و mərəti- اوستایی و mirtis لیتوانیایی هم‌ریشه است. mortārium «هاون» را واتکینز و دِوان از *mr̥-to- «ساییده، کوبیده» می‌گیرند، ولی اِرنو–مِیه می‌نویسند «هیچ ریشه‌شناسی مطمئنی ندارد». mordēre «گزیدن» را پوکورنی و کلاین به گونهٔ گسترش‌یافتهٔ *merd- (قس mardati سنسکریت «می‌کوبد») می‌بندند، اما اِرنو–مِیه هیچ پیوند مطمئنی نمی‌بینند. morbus «بیماری» را کلاین *mor-bʰo- «آنچه می‌فرساید» خوانده، ولی واتکینز می‌گوید «به احتمال بیشتر ریشه‌اش ناشناخته است» و اِرنو–مِیه شباهت آن به morior را تصادفی می‌شمارند. پس ادعای نورایی با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است: یکی از چهار واژه قطعی، دو تا احتمالی، و morbus مشکوک است.

nodes.words: mortal, mortuary, mortgage; mortar; remorse; morbid
nodes.derivation: All six are ordinary Latin > (Old) French > Middle English loans of the words in the parent box. mortal: ME mortal, fr. OF/MF mortel, fr. L. mortalis (: mors, mortis). mortuary: the adj. fr. Late L. mortuarius, the noun fr. ML mortuarium, both to L. mortuus 'dead' (: mors). mortgage: ME morgage, fr. OF mor(t)gage, literally 'dead pledge' - only the first element is Latin mort- ; the second, gage, is Frankish *waddi (Germanic *wadi-, AHD wadh-1 'pledge'), so the word is half-Germanic and Nourai's single arrow from Latin covers only mort-. mortar: partly fr. OE mortere, partly fr. OF mortier, both fr. L. mortarium; the sense 'building mortar' is transferred from the bowl to what was pounded in it (Etymonline, 13c.). remorse: ME remors, fr. MF remors, fr. VL remorsus, pp. of remordere 'to bite again, vex, torment' (re- + mordere) - the metaphor 'the bite of conscience' (Cic. morderi conscientia). morbid: a learned 1650s formation from L. morbidus 'diseased' (: morbus), first 'of the nature of a disease', from 1834 also of mental states.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر شش واژهٔ انگلیسی وام‌واژه‌هایی معمولی از لاتینی‌اند که بیشترشان از راه فرانسهٔ باستان به انگلیسی میانه رسیده‌اند: mortal از mortālis، mortuary از mortuārius/mortuārium (به mortuus «مرده»)، mortar از mortārium (نخست «هاون» و سپس «ملاط» به مناسبت آنچه در هاون می‌کوبیدند)، remorse از remorsus صفت مفعولی remordēre «باز گزیدن، آزردن» (استعارهٔ «گزش وجدان»)، و morbid که واژه‌ای عالمانه از سدهٔ ۱۷ از morbidus است. تنها نکته آنکه mortgage «رهن» دو پاره است: پارهٔ نخست mort- لاتینی است ولی پارهٔ دوم gage از *waddi ژرمنی (فرانکی) است، پس پیکان یگانهٔ نورایی از لاتینی فقط نیمهٔ واژه را توضیح می‌دهد. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: OHG smerzan 'to hurt, ache' (MHG smerzen, NHG schmerzen), with the noun smerzo 'pain', belongs to the s-mobile form *(s)merd- of the root, i.e. to Nourai's 'Smerd' line: Pokorny prints it among the s-forms of mer-d- ('compare the s-forms: gr. smerdnos, smerdaleos terrible, Old High German smerzan ache, smerzo pain', p. 736 f.), and his separate lemma smerd- 'to stink' (p. 970) is expressly said to be a specialisation of the same (s)merd- 'as in NHG schmerzen, Lat. mordere'. Germanic *smert-a-/*smart- shows the regular Grimm outcome of *(s)merd- (d > t, then OHG t > z after r/before nothing... more precisely PGmc t > OHG z by the second sound shift: *smert-an > smerzan). One correction of wording: smerzan is a verb 'to be painful, to ache', so Nourai's gloss 'painful' renders the adjectival sense of the family (OE smeart, OHG smerzo 'pain'), not the verb itself.

nodes.derivation: The root affiliation is right but the arrow is not: English smart is not taken from Old High German, it is the inherited English sibling of smerzan. The verb is ME smerten < OE smeortan 'be painful (of wounds)'; the noun and the adjective are ME smert(e) < OE smeart 'stinging, causing sharp pain' < Germanic *smarta- (Watkins), the same *(s)merd- as OHG smerzan, MDu. smerten, G schmerzen. Nourai's own cited page says so verbatim: Klein 1461 'smart, intr. v. - ME. smerten, fr. OE. smeortan, rel. to MDu. smerten ... OHG. smerzan ... G. schmerzen'. The later English senses ('pert, witty' c. 1300, 'clever' 1620s, 'fashionable' 1718) develop from 'cutting, stinging', and the adjective has no cognate in the sister languages (Etymonline). So: same root, wrong route - a cognate drawn as a descendant.

entries.modern_form: PIE *mers- 'to forget' (Pokorny 6. mer-, mer-s- 'to bother, anger', pp. 737-738; Watkins mers- 'to trouble'; LIV 440 f. *mers-)
entries.note: Root, language label and gloss are right; 'to disturb' is a fair rendering of Pokorny's 'to bother, anger' and of Watkins's 'to trouble', and the two semantic poles of the family are exactly Nourai's two branches: 'forget' (Skt. mrsyate, NP faramus, Lith. mirsti, Arm. moranam, Toch. mars-) and 'hinder, spoil' (Goth. marzjan, OE mierran > mar). One nuance worth recording: Kloekhorst (cited by Wiktionary) takes *mers- to be an s-extension of *mer- 'to die, disappear', which would make Nourai's Mer 2 and Mer 3 one root at bottom; Pokorny (6. mer- separate from 4./5. mer-) and Watkins keep them apart, and so does Nourai.
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *mers- «فراموش کردن» است؛ پوکورنی آن را در ص ۷۳۷–۷۳۸ زیر «6. mer-, mer-s-» با معنای «آزردن، خشمگین کردن» آورده و واتکینز mers- «to trouble». معنای «آشفتن/آشفته کردن» که نورایی داده با هر دو سازگار است، و دو شاخهٔ نمودار او درست همان دو قطب معنایی این خانواده است: «فراموش کردن» (mṛṣyate سنسکریت، فراموش فارسی، miršti لیتوانیایی، moranam ارمنی) و «بازداشتن، تباه کردن» (marzjan گوتی، mierran انگلیسی باستان > mar). نکتهٔ افزودنی آنکه کلوکهورست *mers- را گسترش s-دار ریشهٔ *mer- «مردن، ناپدید شدن» می‌داند که در آن صورت Mer 2 و Mer 3 نورایی در نهایت یک ریشه‌اند؛ اما پوکورنی و واتکینز مانند نورایی آنها را جدا نگه می‌دارند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: The Sanskrit root is real and the glosses are right, but the two compound citation forms are analytic reconstructions, not textbook Sanskrit lemmas. Attested (RV onwards) are mrsyate 'forgets, neglects, bears patiently, forgives', the causative marsayati 'endures, forgives' and the noun marsa- m. 'patient endurance' (Walde-Pokorny II 279; Pokorny 737; EWAia II 332 via Cheung s.v. *mars). Nourai's 'â-marš: to tolerate, be quiet' and 'pra-marš: to forget' are taken over from Horn: Grundriss no. 464 explains NP xamos as 'skr. a + sqrt(mars) geduldig ertragen' and no. 812 explains faramos as 'ai. pra + sqrt(mrs-), mrsyate vergessen'. Huebschmann, writing on the same entry (Pers. Stud. 84), gives the corresponding forms with an asterisk (np. faramust = skr. *pramrsta-, *pramrsti-), i.e. the compound is reconstructed. Methodologically the Persian words are not descendants of Sanskrit anyway but of the parallel Old Iranian *(fra-a-)mrs-; the Sanskrit box stands here as the Indo-Iranian witness.

nodes.derivation: NP xamos/xamus 'silent; extinguished, turned off' does belong to this root in the standard Persian handbooks, but the derivation is Horn's and remains unproven in its detail. Horn no. 464 (p. 103) gives 'xamos schweigend, still ... skr. a + sqrt(mars) geduldig ertragen; vergl. framos (No. 812)', and Mo'in's footnote in Borhan-e Qate' (vol. 2, p. 706/707) repeats it in one line: 'xamos - Sanskrit a-marsa (tolerating, being patient)'. Wiktionary derives it from Middle Persian h'mwsh /xamos/ 'silent' and adds only 'perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mers-', comparing Latvian aizmirst. The weak points are (a) the initial x-, which an Old Iranian preverb *a- cannot give (the MP spelling h'mwsh points to an initial ha-/xa- whose source is unexplained), and (b) the -os-/-us- vocalism, the same difficulty Huebschmann and Henning raise for framos; Cheung's Etymological Dictionary of the Iranian Verb does not list xamos under *mars at all. The meaning 'turned off (of a lamp, a fire)' is a secondary Persian development from 'silent, quiet'. So: right root, route accepted by the Persian tradition but not established.
nodes.derivation_fa: «خاموش» (xāmōš) در سنّت ریشه‌شناسی فارسی به همین ریشه بسته شده، اما بستگیِ جزء‌به‌جزء آن از هرن است و اثبات‌شده نیست. هرن در شمارهٔ ۴۶۴ (ص ۱۰۳) می‌نویسد «xāmōš خاموش، ساکت … skr. ā + √marš (شکیبایی کردن)»، و معین در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع (ج ۲، ص ۷۰۶/۷۰۷) همان را در یک سطر می‌آورد: «خاموش – سانسکریت ā-marṣa (تحمل، صبر کردن)». ویکی‌واژه آن را از فارسی میانهٔ ⟨hʾmwš⟩ xāmōš «ساکت» می‌گیرد و تنها «شاید از *mers- هندواروپایی» می‌افزاید. دو اشکال باقی است: نخست «خ» آغازی که از پیشوند *ā- ایرانی باستان به دست نمی‌آید، و دوم واکهٔ -ōš که همان دشواریِ framōš است و هوبشمان و هنینگ بر آن انگشت گذاشته‌اند؛ چونگ نیز خاموش را زیر *marš نیاورده است. معنای «خاموش (چراغ)» تحول معنایی متأخر فارسی از «ساکت» است. پس ادعای نورایی با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: The derivation is right in substance but the label and the shape of the forms are not what the sources know. The Old Iranian root is mars-/*mrs- 'to forget': Bartholomae's Altiranisches Woerterbuch (cols. 1153-54) has Avestan marsa- adj. 'schwer zu vergessen' and marso.kara-/marsavan- 'das Vergessen bewirkend' (a daeva name), citing np. faramos; Cheung reconstructs Iranian *mars 'to forget' (PIE *mers-, LIV 440 f.). Abolghasemi (FFD p. 65), the reference Nourai cites, writes the ancestor as Old Iranian *fra-a-mrs-ta and *fra-a-mrs-a, not *fra-a-mus-; the -u/o- vocalism of muš is a Middle Persian trait (framos) projected back. And no Old Persian form of this root is attested: Kent's lexicon has only *mer- 'die' (martiya, marta, uva-marsiyus 'by self-death'), nothing for 'forget'. So the node should read Avestan/Old Iranian *mrs-, *fra-a-mrs-, and the 'Old Persian' half of the label is unsupported.

nodes.derivation: MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary has the verb exactly as drawn: 'framustan, framos- [pl(')mwstn' | M pr'mwst, pr'mws-, N fara~] forget', beside the participle 'framos [pl(')mws | M pr'mws, N faramos] forgotten' and the secondary 'framosidan = framustan'. Morphologically the past stem framost/framust continues Old Iranian *fra-a-mrs-ta (fra- 'forth' + a- + zero-grade of *mars-), with the regular Middle Persian loss of the intervocalic prefix vowel and -rs-t- > -st- (FFD p. 65); the present stem framos- shows the -o- that Huebschmann (Pers. Stud. 84) and Henning (1933: 185, quoted by Cheung) found irregular for *mars- and which is usually explained as a rounding/analogical vocalism of the Middle Iranian period. Manichaean MP pr'mws- and Parthian fr'mws- have the same shape, so the form is well attested in both Middle Iranian corpora.

nodes.derivation: New Persian faramus 'forgotten; forgetfulness' continues Middle Persian framos directly; faramusidan/farmosidan is a Dari-period denominal-secondary infinitive built on the present stem (Abolghasemi p. 65: 'فراموشید ... مادهٔ ماضی جعلی است، از مادهٔ مضارع ساخته شده است'), while the older past stem survives in the Classical form faramust/faramesht - which is exactly the word in Nourai's Naser-Khosrow line (nazdik-e xodavand badi nist faramusht). Horn no. 812 (p. 181) lists the whole set 'feramos ..., feramus, feramust, fer(a)mosiden' and cites Vis o Ramin 50.13 for the -iden form; Mo'in's Borhan footnote (vol. 3 p. 1448) and Mann (IEC s.v. mrsio: 'Per. fara-mus, adj. forgetful; fara-musam, inf. -musidan') give the same chain. The variants Nourai prints in Persian script (فرموشیدن، فرامش، فرامشت، فرامشی) are the standard by-forms of the classical language, and Mo'in's Farhang-e Farsi records them under فراموش ('[= فراموش - فرامشت - فرموش]').

nodes.derivation: An empty pass-through box standing for Proto-Germanic *marzjan 'to hinder, offend' (< suffixed o-grade *mors-eyo-), the ancestor of Gothic marzjan 'to offend, cause to stumble', Old Saxon merrian, Old Frisian meria, OHG marren/merren 'to hinder, disturb' and the Old English verb behind mar. Watkins reconstructs exactly this: 'mers-. To trouble. Suffixed o-grade form *mors-eyo- in Germanic *marzjan in Old English merran, mierran, to impede: MAR', and Walde-Pokorny II 279 lists the same Germanic set under mer-s-. The Germanic *z of *marzjan is the regular voicing (Rhotacism after Verner) of the root-final *-s- of *mers- before the *-yo- suffix.

nodes.derivation: English mar 'to damage, spoil' is ME merren/marren (early 13c.) from Old English merran (Anglian) / mierran (West Saxon) 'to waste, spoil, hinder', i.e. from the Germanic *marzjan of the parent box; the a-vocalism of the modern form is the Anglian/dialectal development also seen in marsh (Etymonline). entries.modern_form: Avestan mərəγa- m./n. 'bird (especially of the larger kinds)' (< Proto-Iranian *mr̥gáh, PII *mr̥gás, cf. Skt. mr̥ga- 'wild animal'); the phrase mərəγō saēnō 'the bird Saēna' (Yasht 14.41), saēna- being the name of a large bird of prey, probably the eagle (cf. Skt. śyena- 'eagle, falcon')
entries.note: Language label and the first gloss are right: Bartholomae (AiW col. 1172) heads the entry 'mərəγa- m., n. Vogel, spez. von groesseren' - 'especially of the larger ones', and Buck (Selected Synonyms 3.64, pp. 183-84) writes 'Av. maraya- used of large birds (Barth. 1172), NPers. murgh bird : Skt. mrga- wild animal', which is verbatim Nourai's 'a large bird'. Saēna-mereğa is likewise a real Avestan phrase, but as two words: hau maza mərəγō saēnō 'that great bird Saēna' (Yt. 14.41). The gloss 'dark hawk bird' is where the box goes wrong: saēna- is 'a large bird of prey, probably the eagle' (Bartholomae: 'Name eines grossen Raubvogels, wohl des Adlers'), and Mo'in's Borhan footnote reports that 'scholars translate the word sēn in the Avesta as falcon and eagle'; nothing in the sources supports 'dark'. Also note that this Avestan-headed root box is really an Indo-Iranian noun *mr̥ga-, not a verbal root, and Nourai's own cited KLN:959 does not contain it (see ref_check).

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian murw [mwrw] 'bird' is the regular continuation of Av. mərəγa- / Proto-Iranian *mr̥gáh: the syllabic *r̥ gives Middle Persian ur, and intervocalic/final *-g- is spirantised and written -w (MacKenzie's murw; the same word is Manichaean MP mwrw and Parthian murγ). Nourai's two spellings 'murğ, merv' are two readings of the one Pahlavi grapheme sequence mwrw. The compound sēn-murw [synmwlw] 'a fabulous bird' is Av. mərəγō saēnō with the order reversed and the first element reduced to sēn, and it is the direct source of NP sīmurγ - MacKenzie glosses it '(N sīmurγ)'. The Bundahishn and Menog i Xrad passages Bartholomae and Mo'in quote ('the nest of the bird Sēn (sēnmurw) is on the tree Harwisp-tōxmag') show the word in real Pahlavi context. The gloss 'hawk bird' is acceptable for a bird of prey, though 'the (mythical) bird Sēn' is the accurate rendering.

nodes.derivation: NP murγ/morγ 'bird; (later, specifically) hen' is inherited from MP murw with the restoration of the velar in writing and pronunciation (murw > murγ), and the narrowing 'bird' > 'domestic fowl' is a New Persian development that Mo'in notes explicitly ('در فارسی نیز بمعنی مرغ خانگی (ماکیان) استعمال شود'). sīmurγ is inherited from MP sēnmurw, with the regular Middle > New Persian change of majhūl ē to ī (sēn > sī) and the loss of -n before m in the compound; the popular explanation 'thirty (sī) birds', found in Rashidi and famous from Attar's Manteq al-Tayr, is folk etymology, as Mo'in says of the parallel word sīrang ('ولی این اشتقاق عامیانه است. جزو اول آن سی همان است که در سیمرغ آمده'). nodes.derivation: Sogdian mrγ 'bird' (transliterated marγ; attested in the Buddhist, Manichaean and Christian corpora) is the direct Sogdian reflex of Proto-Iranian *mr̥gáh, with the syllabic *r̥ written simply -r- in the Sogdian script and the velar preserved as -γ. Gharib's Sogdian-Persian-English Dictionary entry 5809-range no. 5432 gives 'mrγ- B, M, S | marγ | Av. mərəγa | ... bird', i.e. Gharib herself derives it from the Avestan word of the root box, and lists the oblique/plural forms (nom. ob. -y, pl. mrγ'yst) and references (GMS 485, 1174, 1182; TSP 2.155, 456 etc.). This is the expected sister-form of Pahlavi murw and Parthian murγ.
